parts.title: Joining a swimming course
parts.setting: A student phones a leisure centre to ask about swimming lessons for beginners.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a student phoning a leisure centre to ask about swimming lessons.
RECEPTIONIST: Good morning, Riverside Leisure Centre. How can I help you?
STUDENT: Good morning. My name is Ana Sharma. I am a first-year student at the university, and I would like to join a swimming course for beginners.
RECEPTIONIST: Of course, Ana. We run beginner courses on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and also on Saturday mornings.
STUDENT: Saturday morning would suit me best. What time does it start?
RECEPTIONIST: The Saturday class starts at half past nine and lasts for one hour.
STUDENT: That sounds good. How long does the whole course last?
RECEPTIONIST: It runs for eight weeks, and there is a short break in the middle for the public holiday weekend.
STUDENT: And how much does it cost?
RECEPTIONIST: The full course is ninety pounds, but students get a discount, so you would pay sixty-five pounds.
STUDENT: That is reasonable. Do I need to bring anything with me?
RECEPTIONIST: Just a swimming costume, a towel, and a pair of goggles if you have them. We provide swimming caps and all the other equipment.
STUDENT: I do not have goggles yet. Can I buy them at the centre?
RECEPTIONIST: Yes, we sell them at reception for eight pounds.
STUDENT: Good. Is there a test before I start, to check my level?
RECEPTIONIST: No test, but the instructor will watch you swim a short distance in the first lesson, just to place you in the right group.
STUDENT: I can swim a little, but I cannot do a proper front crawl yet.
RECEPTIONIST: That is fine. Most beginners are in the same position. The course starts with breathing and floating, then moves on to the basic strokes.
STUDENT: One more thing — is there somewhere to leave my bag while I swim?
RECEPTIONIST: Yes, there are lockers beside the pool. You need a one-pound coin, which you get back afterwards.
STUDENT: How do I book a place?
RECEPTIONIST: You can book online, or I can take your details now and reserve a place for you.
STUDENT: Please reserve a place for me now. My email is ana.sharma@studentmail.com.
RECEPTIONIST: Thank you. I will send you a confirmation email today, and you need to pay by Friday the twentieth of September.
STUDENT: Friday the twentieth — I will make a note of that. Where is the centre, exactly?
RECEPTIONIST: We are on Mill Road, next to the bus station. The nearest bus stop is just outside the main entrance.
STUDENT: Perfect. Thank you very much for your help.
RECEPTIONIST: You are welcome, Ana. We look forward to seeing you on Saturday.

parts.setting: A volunteer welcomes visitors to a guided walk around a riverside park.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a volunteer welcoming visitors to a guided walk around a riverside park.
GUIDE: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Riverside Park. My name is Tom Baker, and I will be your guide for the next hour and a half.
GUIDE: The park was opened in 1924, when the land was given to the town by the Hartley family, who owned the large house you can see across the river.
GUIDE: Before we start, let me tell you a little about the route. We will walk along the river path first, then cross the old stone bridge and come back through the woodland garden.
GUIDE: The whole walk is about two kilometres, and the paths are flat, so it should be comfortable for everyone, including people with pushchairs.
GUIDE: Our first stop is the boathouse, which was built in 1890. In the past, boats carried goods up and down the river, but today the boathouse is used by the local rowing club.
GUIDE: If you look across the water, you can see the heronry. About forty grey herons nest there every spring, and if we are lucky, we may see one fishing in the shallow water near the bank.
GUIDE: Further along the path, we will pass the rose garden. It has more than two hundred varieties of roses, and the best time to see them is in June, when they are all in flower.
GUIDE: The park is also home to a small cafe, the Riverside Cafe, which is open every day from nine in the morning until five in the afternoon. It serves hot drinks, sandwiches, and homemade cakes.
GUIDE: Now, a few practical points. There are toilets near the main entrance and also beside the cafe. Dogs are welcome in the park, but they must be kept on a lead near the children's playground.
GUIDE: The playground was rebuilt last year, and it now has a climbing frame, swings, and a sandpit for younger children.
GUIDE: Each summer, the park hosts a music festival. This year, the festival takes place on the third weekend of July, and entry is free, although visitors are asked to make a small donation.
GUIDE: Finally, if you enjoy today's walk, the Friends of Riverside Park meet on the first Saturday of every month to help with planting and litter picking. New members are always welcome.
GUIDE: Right, let us begin. Please follow me down to the river path, and do watch your step on the wooden bridge — it can be slippery after rain.

parts.title: Planning a presentation on renewable energy
parts.setting: Two students discuss their group presentation with their tutor.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear two students discussing a group presentation with their tutor.
TUTOR: Good afternoon, Maya and Daniel. How is your group presentation coming along?
MAYA: It is going well, Dr Evans. We have decided to focus on renewable energy in small towns, and Daniel has found some very useful data.
DANIEL: Yes, I looked at three towns in the north of England that now get most of their electricity from wind and solar power.
TUTOR: That sounds like a good angle. How long is the presentation?
MAYA: Twenty minutes, plus five minutes for questions from the class.
TUTOR: And how have you divided the work between you?
DANIEL: I will introduce the topic and explain how wind turbines work. Maya will talk about solar power and the costs, and then we will present our conclusions together.
MAYA: We have also made a short video of an interview with the manager of a wind farm near Leeds. We would like to show a two-minute clip from it.
TUTOR: That could work well, but make sure the clip adds something new. Do not just repeat what you have already said.
DANIEL: Good point. The manager talks about the problems they faced when the wind farm was built, which we have not covered in the main talk.
TUTOR: Excellent. What about your sources? Have you used enough academic material?
MAYA: We have used two journal articles and a government report from last year. I was worried that might not be enough.
TUTOR: Three good sources are fine for a twenty-minute talk, but make sure you list them all on your final slide.
DANIEL: We also wanted to include a graph showing how electricity prices have changed over the last ten years. Is that a good idea?
TUTOR: Yes, a clear graph is always helpful, but keep it simple — no more than three lines on one graph.
MAYA: When is the deadline for the slides?
TUTOR: You need to send me the slides by Thursday evening, so I can check them before your presentation on Monday morning.
DANIEL: Monday morning — that is the ninth of June, is it not?
TUTOR: Yes, the ninth of June, at ten o'clock, in Room 4 of the Science Building.
MAYA: One more question. Should we give the class a handout?
TUTOR: A one-page summary would be useful, but do not print the whole presentation. Just the main points and your three sources.
DANIEL: Thanks, Dr Evans. We will send you the slides on Thursday.
TUTOR: Good. I am looking forward to it.

parts.title: Sleep and memory
parts.setting: A university lecturer gives a talk about how sleep affects memory.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a lecture about sleep and memory.
LECTURER: Good morning. Today I want to talk about something that affects every student in this room: the link between sleep and memory.
LECTURER: Most of us think of sleep as a time when the brain switches off. In fact, the brain is extremely busy while we sleep, and one of its most important jobs is to organise what we have learned during the day.
LECTURER: Sleep has two main stages that matter for memory. The first is deep sleep, which happens mostly in the first half of the night. During deep sleep, the brain moves new facts — like the names and dates you studied — from short-term storage into long-term memory.
LECTURER: The second stage is REM sleep, which stands for rapid eye movement sleep. This happens mostly in the second half of the night, and it seems to be important for skills and for emotional memories.
LECTURER: A famous experiment at Harvard University showed this very clearly. Two groups of students were taught a new skill in the evening. One group slept normally, while the other group stayed awake all night. The next morning, the group that had slept performed twenty per cent better on the test.
LECTURER: So what does this mean for students? First, it means that staying up all night before an exam is usually a bad idea. You may feel that you have studied more, but without sleep, much of that information will not be stored properly.
LECTURER: Second, short naps can help. A nap of twenty to thirty minutes in the afternoon can improve your ability to remember new words, although a nap longer than an hour can leave you feeling sleepy.
LECTURER: Third, regular sleep matters more than one good night. Students who sleep seven to eight hours every night remember more over a whole term than students whose sleep changes a lot from night to night.
LECTURER: Finally, what you do before bed matters too. Reading your notes for fifteen minutes in the evening, and then going to sleep, is more effective than reading the same notes for an hour in the morning.
LECTURER: To sum up, sleep is not wasted time. It is part of learning itself. If you want to remember what you study, protect your sleep as carefully as you protect your study time.

NARRATOR: You will hear a student phoning a letting agent about a flat.
AGENT: Good afternoon, City Lets. This is James speaking. How can I help?
STUDENT: Hello, my name is Ben Carter. I am looking for a one-bedroom flat near the university, and I saw your advertisement for a flat on Oak Street.
AGENT: Yes, the Oak Street flat is still available. It is on the second floor, and it is about a ten-minute walk from the main campus.
STUDENT: That sounds ideal. How much is the rent?
AGENT: The rent is five hundred and fifty pounds a month, and that includes water and heating, but not electricity.
STUDENT: Is there a deposit?
AGENT: Yes, the deposit is one month's rent, and you will get it back at the end of the tenancy if there is no damage to the flat.
STUDENT: When could I move in?
AGENT: The flat is available from the first of October. The current tenant is moving out at the end of September.
STUDENT: Could I come and see the flat this week?
AGENT: Of course. I can show you round on Wednesday afternoon at three o'clock, or on Thursday morning at eleven.
STUDENT: Wednesday at three would be perfect. What is the flat like inside?
AGENT: It is quite small but very bright. There is a living room with a sofa and a small dining table, a separate kitchen, and a bathroom with a shower. There is no bath, I am afraid.
STUDENT: Is there internet in the flat?
AGENT: Not yet, but the previous tenant had broadband, so the connection is already there. You would just need to choose a provider.
STUDENT: And is there any parking?
AGENT: There is no private parking, but you can park on the street with a resident's permit, which costs forty pounds a year from the council.
STUDENT: I do not have a car, so that does not matter. Is the area quiet at night?
AGENT: Yes, Oak Street is a quiet residential street, and most of the neighbours are families and postgraduate students.
STUDENT: That sounds good. Can I bring a friend to the viewing on Wednesday?
AGENT: Certainly. Just meet me outside the main entrance at three o'clock, and please bring some photo identification with you.
STUDENT: I will bring my passport. Thank you very much.
AGENT: You are welcome, Ben. I will see you on Wednesday.

parts.setting: A guide introduces visitors to a university botanical garden.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a guide introducing visitors to a botanical garden.
GUIDE: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the university botanical garden. My name is Dr Helen Wright, and I manage the garden's education programme.
GUIDE: The garden covers twelve hectares, and it is home to more than eight thousand different kinds of plants, from tiny alpine flowers to trees that are over two hundred years old.
GUIDE: The garden was founded in 1831 as a place where medical students could learn about plants used in medicine. Today, it is used for teaching, research, and by the public, who are welcome to visit free of charge.
GUIDE: We will begin our tour in the glasshouses, where the temperature is kept at twenty-five degrees all year round. Inside, you will see plants from tropical rainforests, including orchids, palms, and a banana tree that produces fruit every summer.
GUIDE: From there, we will walk to the rock garden, which was built in 1935 from stone brought from the mountains of Wales. The small plants that grow there come from high places all over the world, where the summers are short and the winters are very cold.
GUIDE: Next, we will visit the herb garden. Many of the herbs here have been used as medicines for hundreds of years. For example, the leaves of the foxglove plant were once used to treat heart problems, and they are still the source of an important modern drug.
GUIDE: After the herb garden, we will stop at the lake, where you can see water lilies and a family of ducks that has lived here for many years. Please do not feed the ducks, as bread can make them ill.
GUIDE: The garden is open every day from ten in the morning until six in the evening, except on Christmas Day. The best time to visit is in May, when the spring flowers are at their best and the trees are full of blossom.
GUIDE: Before we start, let me mention the garden shop, which sells seeds, books, and plants grown here in the garden. All the money from the shop goes back into looking after the garden.
GUIDE: Finally, if you would like to learn more, we run a short course on gardening for beginners every Saturday morning in the autumn. The course costs thirty pounds for six weeks, and you can sign up at the visitor centre.
GUIDE: Now, if everyone is ready, please follow me into the first glasshouse, and mind the step as you go in — it is a little higher than it looks.

parts.setting: A university lecturer gives a talk about honeybees and their role in farming.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a lecture about honeybees and pollination.
LECTURER: Good afternoon. In today's lecture, I want to look at one of the most important animals in agriculture: the honeybee.
LECTURER: Most people know that bees make honey, but their real value lies in pollination. When a bee visits a flower to collect nectar, pollen sticks to its body, and when the bee moves to the next flower, some of that pollen is left behind. This allows the plant to produce seeds and fruit.
LECTURER: Around three quarters of the world's food crops depend on pollinators to some extent. Crops such as apples, almonds, and coffee all produce much smaller harvests without bees.
LECTURER: Unfortunately, honeybee numbers have been falling in many countries. In the United States, for example, beekeepers have lost about forty per cent of their colonies in some recent winters.
LECTURER: There are several reasons for this decline. The first is the loss of habitat. As more land is used for housing and for large fields of a single crop, bees have fewer wild flowers to feed on.
LECTURER: The second reason is pesticides. Some chemicals used to protect crops from insects can also harm bees, damaging their ability to find their way back to the hive.
LECTURER: The third reason is disease. A tiny mite called Varroa attacks young bees and spreads viruses through the colony. Beekeepers now have to treat their hives regularly to keep this mite under control.
LECTURER: What can be done? Farmers can help by planting strips of wild flowers along the edges of their fields. Studies have shown that these flower strips can increase the number of wild bees in an area by up to fifty per cent.
LECTURER: Gardeners can help too, by growing plants that flower at different times of the year, so that bees always have food. Even a small balcony with a few pots can make a difference.
LECTURER: Finally, scientists are working on new ways to protect bees, including breeding bees that are more resistant to the Varroa mite and developing safer pesticides.
LECTURER: To conclude, bees are not just honey producers. They are essential workers in our food system, and protecting them is one of the simplest ways to protect our food supply.

parts.setting: A lecturer explains how tides work.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a lecture about the science of tides.
LECTURER: Good morning. Today I would like to talk about tides — the regular rise and fall of the sea that has fascinated sailors, fishermen and scientists for centuries. The main cause of tides is the gravitational pull of the Moon. As the Moon orbits the Earth, its gravity pulls the ocean towards it, creating a bulge of water on the side of the Earth facing the Moon. At the same time, a second bulge forms on the opposite side, because the Earth is pulled towards the Moon slightly more strongly than the water on the far side. As the Earth rotates, different places pass through these two bulges, and that is why most coastal areas experience two high tides and two low tides each day. The Sun also affects the tides, although its influence is weaker because it is much further away. When the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are in a straight line, which happens at the new moon and the full moon, their gravitational forces combine. The result is a spring tide, with higher high tides and lower low tides than usual. The name has nothing to do with the season of spring — it comes from an old word meaning to rise up. In contrast, when the Sun and the Moon are at right angles to each other, their forces partly cancel out, and we get a neap tide, with a smaller difference between high and low water. Neap tides occur during the first and third quarters of the Moon. The height of a tide also depends on local geography. In a narrow bay, the incoming water has nowhere to spread, so it can rise much higher than on an open coast. The Bay of Fundy in Canada is famous for this: the difference between high and low tide there can reach sixteen metres, the largest in the world. Tides are not just a curiosity — they have shaped human life for thousands of years. Fishing communities planned their work around the tide tables, and today engineers are building tidal power stations that generate electricity from the movement of the water. Understanding tides, therefore, is both a scientific challenge and a practical necessity.

parts.title: A tour of the Old Station Railway Museum
parts.setting: A guide welcomes visitors to a small railway museum and describes the tour.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a guide welcoming visitors to a small railway museum.
GUIDE: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Old Station Railway Museum. My name is Daniel, and I will be your guide this morning. Before we begin, let me tell you a little about this building. The station opened in eighteen eighty-four, and trains stopped here for almost one hundred years. The last passenger train left in nineteen eighty-one, and the building stood empty for ten years before a group of local volunteers saved it and turned it into a museum.
Our tour today will last about one hour, and we will visit four rooms. We start here, in the ticket hall, where passengers once bought their tickets. You can still see the original wooden ticket counter, and the old timetable boards on the wall. The earliest timetable we have is from eighteen ninety-two, and it shows just six trains a day.
Next, we will go into the waiting room, which has been restored to look exactly as it did in nineteen twenty. The benches, the stove, and even the posters on the wall are all original. In those days, passengers waited here for hours, because trains were often delayed in winter.
After that, we visit the signal box, where you can try pulling the levers that once controlled the signals and the points. Please be careful with the levers — they are heavy, and some of them are over a hundred years old.
Finally, we will go outside to the platform, where our oldest exhibit is waiting: a steam locomotive called the Green Dragon, built in nineteen oh three. It carried coal from the mines to the port for forty years. You are welcome to climb into the driver's cab and have your photograph taken, but please do not touch the controls.
The museum is open from Tuesday to Sunday, from ten in the morning until four in the afternoon. Admission is free, but we do ask visitors to leave a small donation if they can. There is a small cafe in the old parcels office, and it serves tea, coffee, and homemade cakes. The shop sells postcards, books, and model trains.
Before we start, please remember that photography is allowed everywhere in the museum, but please do not use a flash in the waiting room, because the light can damage the old posters. If you have any questions during the tour, please just ask. Let us begin in the ticket hall.

parts.setting: Two students plan their arguments for a class debate about social media.

NARRATOR: You will hear two students planning a class debate about social media.
JAMES: Hi Lena. Have you started preparing for the debate on Friday?
LENA: A little. Our team has to argue that social media does more harm than good for teenagers. I am not sure where to begin.
JAMES: Let us start with the strongest point: time. The average teenager spends more than three hours a day on social media, and that time comes straight out of homework, sleep, and sport.
LENA: That is a good point, but the other team will say that teenagers also learn a lot online. How do we answer that?
JAMES: We can say that learning is different from scrolling. Most of those three hours are spent watching short videos.
LENA: True. What about mental health? I read a survey that found teenagers who spend more than two hours a day on social media are more likely to report feeling anxious.
JAMES: Yes, that survey was done last year with five thousand teenagers. We can quote it — but we need to be careful, because the other team may say the survey only shows a link, not a cause.
LENA: We can accept that, and still argue that the link is strong enough to worry parents and teachers.
JAMES: Good. Another point is sleep. Many teenagers check their phones late at night, and the light from the screen makes it harder to fall asleep.
LENA: And tired teenagers do worse at school the next day.
JAMES: What about the other side? The opposing team will say social media helps teenagers keep in touch with friends and family.
LENA: That is true, especially for teenagers who live far from their friends. But we can argue that real conversations are better than messages, and that many teenagers already meet their friends at school every day.
JAMES: We should also mention online bullying. It is harder to escape than bullying in the playground, because it can follow you home.
LENA: That is our strongest emotional point. We should keep it for the end, so the audience remembers it.
JAMES: Agreed. So our order is: time, mental health, sleep, and then bullying at the end. Who will speak first?
LENA: You should open, because you are good at introductions. I will take the mental health and sleep points, and you can finish with bullying.
JAMES: Fine. Let us meet on Wednesday evening to practise. We need to keep each speech under four minutes.
LENA: Wednesday at seven in the library. I will bring the survey results, and you bring the notes on sleep.
JAMES: Perfect. See you then.

parts.title: Urban trees and city heat
parts.setting: A lecturer explains how trees help cities cope with rising temperatures.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a lecture about how trees help cities cope with rising temperatures.
LECTURER: Good morning. Today I want to talk about a simple and surprisingly powerful tool for cooling our cities: the urban tree. As cities grow hotter, researchers are paying more attention to the shade and cooling that trees provide.
First, let us look at the problem. Cities are usually several degrees warmer than the countryside around them. This is called the urban heat island effect. Roads, roofs, and pavements absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, so the city never fully cools down. During a heatwave, this difference can reach seven degrees, which puts elderly people and young children at serious risk.
Trees cool a city in two ways. The first is shade. A large tree can shade an area of more than one hundred square metres, and the ground beneath it can be ten degrees cooler than the same ground in full sun. The second is evaporation. A mature tree releases hundreds of litres of water into the air each day through its leaves, and as this water evaporates, it takes heat with it. Together, shade and evaporation can lower the temperature of a street by two to five degrees.
Trees also clean the air by trapping dust and absorbing some pollutants. They reduce noise from traffic, and they give people somewhere pleasant to walk and sit. Studies have found that patients in rooms with a view of trees recover faster than patients whose windows face a brick wall.
However, planting trees in cities is not easy. The soil under a pavement is often too shallow and too dry, and the roots have little room to grow. Many young trees die within five years of planting, because nobody waters them during the first dry summer. To succeed, a city needs to choose the right species — trees that can survive drought, pollution, and salty roads in winter — and it needs to water them for at least the first three years.
Some cities are now taking this seriously. In Singapore, planners aim to plant one million more trees by twenty thirty. In Paris, the city is planting trees along every street it rebuilds. These programmes are expensive, but researchers argue that planting a tree costs far less than treating heat-related illness, or cooling a building with air conditioning.
To conclude, urban trees are not decoration. They are infrastructure — as important to a healthy city as clean water or reliable transport. The question is not whether we can afford to plant them, but whether we can afford not to.

GUIDE: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the City Museum. My name is Sarah Collins, and I will be your guide for the next hour.

GUIDE: Before we start, let me tell you a little about the route. We will begin in the Roman gallery on the ground floor, then go upstairs to the Victorian rooms, and finish in the modern art gallery.

GUIDE: Upstairs, the Victorian rooms show how a wealthy family lived in 1890. The furniture, the clothes and even the children's toys are all original.
GUIDE: The modern art gallery on the top floor changes its exhibition four times a year. The current exhibition shows photographs of the city taken over the last fifty years.
GUIDE: Please feel free to take photographs in the museum, but do not use a flash, because the light can damage the old fabrics and papers.
GUIDE: We will finish the tour in the museum cafe, where you can buy tea, coffee and light lunches. The cafe is open from ten in the morning until four in the afternoon.
GUIDE: There is also a small gift shop next to the cafe. It sells books, postcards and copies of some of the objects you will see today.
GUIDE: The museum is closed on Mondays, and it is open from Tuesday to Sunday, from ten in the morning until five in the afternoon.
GUIDE: If you have any questions during the tour, please ask me at any time. Let us begin in the Roman gallery.

parts.title: The history of the bicycle
parts.setting: A lecturer talks about the history of the bicycle.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a lecture about the history of the bicycle.
LECTURER: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about the bicycle, a machine that changed the way ordinary people travelled, and which is now used by more than a billion people around the world.
LECTURER: The first bicycle appeared in Germany in 1817. It was called the draisine, after its inventor, Karl Drais. It had two wheels and a wooden frame, but it had no pedals. The rider pushed it along with his feet, like a scooter.
LECTURER: The draisine was not a great success. It was heavy, it was difficult to steer, and it was soon forgotten. But the idea of a two-wheeled machine did not disappear.
LECTURER: In the 1860s, a new design appeared in France. It had pedals attached to the front wheel, and it was called the velocipede, which means fast foot in Latin. It was made of wood and iron, and it was so uncomfortable that riders called it the boneshaker.
LECTURER: The next big change came in the 1870s, with the penny-farthing. This bicycle had a very large front wheel and a very small back wheel. The large wheel meant that one turn of the pedals took the rider a long way, so the bicycle could travel fast.
LECTURER: The penny-farthing was fast, but it was also dangerous. The rider sat very high above the ground, and if the front wheel hit a stone, the rider could fall forwards over the handlebars.
LECTURER: The modern bicycle arrived in 1885, with the safety bicycle. It had two wheels of the same size, a chain that drove the back wheel, and pneumatic tyres filled with air, which made the ride much more comfortable.
LECTURER: The safety bicycle was a huge success. Within ten years, cycling had become a popular pastime, and bicycles were being made in factories in Britain, France, Germany and the United States.
LECTURER: The bicycle also changed society. For the first time, working people could travel easily to jobs in other towns. It also gave women a new freedom, because a woman on a bicycle could travel alone, without a horse or a carriage.
LECTURER: In the twentieth century, the bicycle had to compete with the car, and in many countries it became less common. But in recent years, cycling has become popular again, partly because of worries about health and the environment, and partly because cities have built safe cycle lanes.
LECTURER: Today, the bicycle is still changing. Electric bicycles, which have a small motor to help the rider, are now the fastest-growing type of bicycle in Europe. The simple machine that Karl Drais invented in 1817 is still with us, in a new form.

MARIA: The report is due on the twenty-second of March, and it must be about two thousand five hundred words long.

parts.title: Volcanoes and how they erupt
parts.setting: A lecturer talks about volcanoes and how they erupt.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a lecture about volcanoes and how they erupt.
LECTURER: Good morning. Today we are going to look at volcanoes: what they are, why they erupt, and what happens when they do.
LECTURER: A volcano is an opening in the surface of the Earth, through which hot, melted rock, gas and ash can escape. The melted rock below the surface is called magma. When it reaches the surface, it is called lava.
LECTURER: Volcanoes usually form where two of the Earth's plates meet. The plates are huge pieces of rock that move very slowly, a few centimetres a year. When one plate moves under another, the rock melts and forms magma.
LECTURER: Not all volcanoes are the same. Some erupt quietly, with lava flowing slowly down the sides. Others explode violently, throwing ash and rock high into the sky.
LECTURER: The type of eruption depends on the magma. If the magma is thin and runny, the gas inside it can escape easily, and the eruption is gentle. If the magma is thick and sticky, the gas cannot escape, pressure builds up, and the volcano explodes.
LECTURER: One of the most famous eruptions in history was the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in the year 79. The volcano buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash, and the towns were not discovered again for more than fifteen hundred years.
LECTURER: Another famous eruption was Krakatoa, in Indonesia, in 1883. The explosion was so loud that it was heard three thousand kilometres away, and it destroyed most of the island.
LECTURER: Volcanoes can also affect the climate. When a volcano erupts, it can throw tiny particles of ash and gas into the atmosphere. These particles reflect sunlight back into space, and the Earth becomes cooler for a year or two.

parts.setting: A lecturer talks about how earthquakes are measured.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a lecture about how earthquakes are measured.
LECTURER: Good afternoon. Today we are going to look at how scientists measure earthquakes, and what the numbers they use actually mean.
LECTURER: An earthquake happens when the rocks below the surface of the Earth suddenly move. The place where the movement starts, deep underground, is called the focus. The point on the surface directly above the focus is called the epicentre.
LECTURER: When the rocks move, they send out waves of energy in all directions, rather like the ripples that spread out when you drop a stone into a pond. These waves travel through the Earth, and they can be felt hundreds of kilometres away.
LECTURER: Scientists measure earthquakes with an instrument called a seismometer. A seismometer is a very sensitive machine that can detect even the smallest movements of the ground. The record it produces is called a seismogram.
LECTURER: For many years, the strength of an earthquake was measured on the Richter scale, which was invented in 1935 by Charles Richter, an American scientist. The Richter scale goes from one to ten, and each whole number is ten times stronger than the number below it.
LECTURER: So an earthquake of magnitude six is ten times stronger than an earthquake of magnitude five, and one hundred times stronger than an earthquake of magnitude four. That is why a small increase in the number can mean a very big increase in the damage.
LECTURER: Today, scientists usually use a different scale, called the moment magnitude scale. This scale measures the total energy released by the earthquake, and it is more accurate for very large earthquakes.
LECTURER: The largest earthquake ever recorded was in Chile in 1960. It had a magnitude of nine point five, and it caused a tsunami, a huge sea wave, which travelled across the Pacific Ocean.
LECTURER: The depth of an earthquake is also important. A shallow earthquake, with a focus close to the surface, usually causes more damage than a deep earthquake of the same magnitude, because the energy has less far to travel.
LECTURER: Most earthquakes are too small to feel. In fact, scientists estimate that about five hundred thousand earthquakes happen every year, but only about one hundred thousand of them can be felt by people, and only about one hundred cause serious damage.
LECTURER: By measuring earthquakes carefully, scientists can learn where the dangerous areas are, and they can help engineers to design buildings that are strong enough to survive an earthquake. That is why measurement matters.

SECRETARY: Good evening, Hilltop Walking Club. How can I help you?
STUDENT: Good evening. My name is Laura Bennett. I have just moved to the area, and I would like to join your walking club.

SECRETARY: We meet every Saturday morning. We gather at the market square at nine o'clock, and we usually finish by one o'clock in the afternoon.
STUDENT: How far do you usually walk?

STUDENT: How much does it cost to join?
SECRETARY: Membership costs twenty-five pounds a year. That includes insurance, and a copy of our walks programme, which is published four times a year.
STUDENT: Is there a walk this Saturday that I could join, to try it out?
SECRETARY: Yes, this Saturday we are walking from the market square to Willow Lake, which is about ten kilometres. It is an easy walk, mostly flat, so it would be a good first walk.
STUDENT: That sounds perfect. What time should I arrive?
SECRETARY: Please arrive at the market square by quarter to nine, so we can start on time. Look for the group with the green flag.
STUDENT: I will be there. Is there anything else I should know?
SECRETARY: Just one thing: if the weather is very bad, we cancel the walk. We announce cancellations on our website by eight o'clock on Saturday morning.
STUDENT: Thank you very much for your help.
SECRETARY: You are welcome, Laura. We look forward to meeting you on Saturday.

NARRATOR: You will hear a guide welcoming visitors to a tour of a historic house.
GUIDE: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Ashford House. My name is Peter Green, and I will show you around the house today.
GUIDE: Ashford House was built in 1740, for the Ashford family, who were wealthy wool merchants. The family lived here for over two hundred years, until 1965, when the last member of the family died.
GUIDE: The house was then given to the National Trust, which opened it to the public in 1970. About sixty thousand people visit the house every year.
GUIDE: We will start in the entrance hall, which is the oldest part of the house. The stone floor and the wooden staircase are both original, from 1740.
GUIDE: From the hall, we will go into the drawing room, which was used for entertaining guests. The paintings on the walls show members of the Ashford family, and the furniture is from the eighteenth century.
GUIDE: Next, we will visit the dining room. The family ate their main meal here every evening at seven o'clock, and the table could seat sixteen people.
GUIDE: Upstairs, there are six bedrooms. The largest bedroom belonged to the head of the family, and it has a wonderful view over the gardens.
GUIDE: The gardens are also worth a visit. They were designed in 1780, and they cover about twenty acres. There is a lake, a rose garden, and a long path lined with trees.
GUIDE: The tour will take about one hour. After the tour, you are free to walk in the gardens, and you can visit the tea room, which is open from eleven in the morning until five in the afternoon.
GUIDE: Please do not touch the furniture or the paintings, because they are very old and easily damaged. Photography is allowed in the gardens, but not inside the house.
GUIDE: The house is open from Wednesday to Sunday, from ten in the morning until five in the afternoon. It is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays.
GUIDE: If you have any questions during the tour, please ask me. Let us start in the entrance hall.

parts.setting: Two students discuss their presentation on plastic recycling.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear two students discussing their presentation on plastic recycling.
TUTOR: Good morning. You are going to give a presentation on plastic recycling next week. How is your preparation going?
LUCY: We have done most of the research, but we still need to decide how to organise the presentation.
TUTOR: What have you found out so far?
SAM: We found that about nine million tonnes of plastic are thrown away in this country every year, and only about thirty percent of it is recycled.
TUTOR: That is a surprising figure. What happens to the rest?
LUCY: Most of it is buried in the ground, in landfill sites, and some of it is burned. A small amount ends up in rivers and in the sea.
TUTOR: And what are the problems with plastic in the sea?
SAM: Sea animals can eat small pieces of plastic, and they can die. Plastic also breaks into tiny pieces, which are very difficult to remove from the water.
TUTOR: What solutions will you talk about?
LUCY: We will talk about three solutions. First, people should use less plastic, for example by carrying their own shopping bags. Second, more types of plastic should be recycled. Third, companies should design products that use less plastic packaging.
TUTOR: Good. How long will the presentation be?
SAM: It will be twenty minutes long, followed by ten minutes for questions from the audience.
TUTOR: And how will you divide the presentation between you?
LUCY: Sam will introduce the topic and explain the problem, and I will talk about the solutions and the conclusion.
TUTOR: Will you use any visual aids?
SAM: Yes, we will use slides, with charts showing how much plastic is recycled, and photographs of plastic in the sea. We will also bring some examples of recycled products.
TUTOR: That sounds good. When will you practise the presentation?
LUCY: We will practise on Thursday afternoon, in room twelve, and we would like you to watch us, if you have time.
TUTOR: I will be happy to watch. Please send me your slides by Wednesday evening, so I can look at them first.
SAM: Thank you. We will send them on Wednesday.

parts.title: The history of photography
parts.setting: A lecturer talks about the history of photography.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a lecture about the history of photography.
LECTURER: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about the history of photography, from the first photographs in the nineteenth century to the digital cameras we use today.
LECTURER: The first successful photograph was taken in France in 1826, by Joseph Nicéphore Niépce. He used a metal plate covered with a chemical that changed when light fell on it. The photograph took eight hours to make, because the chemical was not very sensitive to light.
LECTURER: A few years later, in 1839, Louis Daguerre invented a new method, called the daguerreotype. This method was much faster: a photograph took only a few minutes. The daguerreotype became very popular, and many people had their portraits taken.
LECTURER: However, the daguerreotype had a problem. Each photograph was unique: there was only one copy, and it could not be copied. This changed in the 1840s, when William Henry Fox Talbot invented a method that used a negative, from which many positive prints could be made.
LECTURER: For the next hundred years, photography used film. A roll of film could hold thirty-six photographs, and the film had to be taken to a shop to be developed. People usually waited several days before they saw their photographs.
LECTURER: Colour photography became common in the 1960s, although colour photographs had existed since the early twentieth century. At first, colour film was expensive, and many people continued to use black and white film.
LECTURER: The next big change was the digital camera, which appeared in the 1990s. A digital camera does not use film. Instead, it records the picture as numbers, and the picture can be seen immediately on the back of the camera.
LECTURER: At first, digital cameras were expensive, and the quality of the pictures was not very good. But the quality improved quickly, and by the early 2000s, digital cameras were more popular than film cameras.
LECTURER: Today, most photographs are taken with a mobile phone. The first phone with a camera appeared in the year 2000, and now almost every phone has a camera. It is estimated that more than one trillion photographs are taken every year around the world.
LECTURER: Photography has changed the way we remember our lives. Before photography, most people had no picture of themselves at all. Today, we take photographs every day, and we share them with people all over the world in seconds.
LECTURER: And yet, the basic idea has not changed since 1826: light falls on a sensitive surface, and a picture is made. The technology has changed, but the idea is the same.
